[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey (WVS) data merged with national Gini coefficients and GDP per capita, analyzing interaction effects of collectivism (e.g., from Hofstede's dimensions) on the relationship between perceived social support and subjective well-being. — This allows direct testing of whether the moderation effect of collectivism and income inequality on the social support–wellbeing link is significant beyond the effect of GDP per capita, using multilevel modeling to account for country-level variation.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel studies from East Asian (e.g., Japan, South Korea) and Latin American (e.g., Brazil, Mexico) collectivist societies with high income inequality, measuring perceived social support, subjective wellbeing (e.g., life satisfaction, positive affect), and objective economic indicators. — Such panel data can establish temporal precedence and within-person effects, reducing confounding from cross-sectional comparisons, and directly test if social support explains more variance in wellbeing changes than GDP per capita changes in these specific contexts.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on social support and subjective wellbeing in collectivist vs. individualist cultures, stratified by income inequality levels, with a focus on controlling for GDP per capita. — A systematic synthesis of prior evidence can reveal whether the hypothesized conditional effect is consistently observed across studies, and identify gaps or contradictions in the current literature, thereby confirming or refuting the scope condition.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies on the impact of local environmental improvements (e.g., urban greening, pollution reduction) on self-reported life satisfaction in high-trust, high-income communities, compared to equivalent income changes. — Causal evidence from natural experiments or randomized interventions can isolate the effect of environmental quality from GDP, testing whether the effect is indeed stronger in the specified context.

[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey (WVS) and Gallup World Poll data for OECD countries (2000-2020) combined with city-level air quality indices and GDP per capita — These datasets allow multi-level modeling to isolate the variance in subjective wellbeing explained by environmental quality (e.g., PM2.5, green space access) relative to GDP per capita, controlling for income levels. This directly tests the comparative explanatory power across all income brackets.

[PATH:literature] OECD Better Life Index and Environmental Performance Index (EPI) longitudinal studies — Existing meta-analyses and panel studies using these indices often report effect sizes for environmental factors on life satisfaction. A systematic review or replication analysis can quantify whether environmental quality consistently accounts for as much variance as GDP per capita across income groups, addressing the disputed claim.

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiments of environmental policy changes (e.g., London Congestion Charge, German autobahn speed limits) with pre/post wellbeing surveys — Such quasi-experimental designs provide causal evidence of environmental quality improvements on subjective wellbeing. Comparing these effects to income shocks (e.g., tax rebates) across income strata can reveal if environmental quality rivals GDP per capita in explanatory power, especially for lower-income groups.
